title: Guilt about missing
hook: missed days need no speech: the prodigal son's rehearsed apology never gets finished, because the father runs first
tomorrow: two poems went up on a monastery wall. which one won the robe?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: fresh form. The boy's whistle was new; the prayer under it was not. Today's break: not boredom, but days gone missing.

Ever rehearse an apology in the shower, word by word? In a parable in Luke, a younger son has spent his whole inheritance and ends up feeding pigs, starving. He writes his speech in his head: "Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants." Then he walks home. Read what he actually says when he gets there, in the King James text. The last line is missing.
screen: `AN APOLOGY REHEARSED IN THE SHOWER.` → `FEEDING PIGS, STARVING.` → `MAKE ME A HIRED SERVANT.` → `THE LAST LINE IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: Here's why. "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." The son starts the speech anyway. He gets as far as no more worthy to be called thy son. And the father turns to the servants: "Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him." The bargaining line, make me a hired servant, never gets said. The father doesn't need it. That's the Christian teaching of repentance and grace. Turning back, what Christians call repentance, starts when the son comes to himself and stands up to go home. And grace meets him before his explanation is done. The father ran first. The parable doesn't pretend nothing happened; in the next scene the older brother is still angry. But the welcome doesn't wait for the speech. Missed days in a practice work the same way. Guilt wants a speech: why you stopped, how you'll make up for it, how you'll never miss again. The parable says the road home is enough.
screen: `THE FATHER RAN.` · `BRING FORTH THE BEST ROBE.` · `THE BARGAINING LINE NEVER SAID.` · `GRACE BEFORE THE EXPLANATION.` · then, large: `JUST START AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Open the notebook or the place where you practice, and write only today's date at the top. No account of the missed days, no promises to make up for them. Then sit for the rest of the time, simply back.
Guilt about missing: the urge to explain missed days before coming back, which the prodigal son's father never waited to hear.
Your line: just start again. The father ran before the speech was done. Welcome back to day 1675.

howItsDone: Christians read the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15) as a picture of repentance and grace. On a personal rule, a restart after missed days is simply beginning again on the next day.

fork.setup: your friend skipped choir for a month and wants to email the director a long apology before showing up. what would the parable suggest?
options: just show up at the next rehearsal; the welcome doesn't wait for the speech.

fork.reveal: the father ran out before his son finished apologizing, and called for the best robe. the road home was enough.

chat.meaning: In Luke's parable the father ran to his son and cut off the rehearsed speech. In Christian teaching, grace meets you on the road home.

tie.story: The prodigal son rehearsed a speech, but his father ran to him and called for the best robe before he finished.
